seep.text:
The boat is pulled into a shingle cove while the master waits for the wind to turn. Above the tideline there is a seep of fresh water in the rock, and a track of birds going down to it.

One of the men looks at the birds. Another looks at the water. Nobody tells you which is the better use of an hour.

choices.text: Fill every skin at the seep.
Hunt the reeds with one of the men.

watered.text:
The skins fill slowly, one held under the seep while another is stoppered and passed back to the boat. The water tastes of stone and is colder than the sea.

By the time the last skin is full, the master has the oars out. You carry the hour aboard with you: a small, ordinary thing done well.

hunted.text:
The reeds are waist-high and full of small noise. The man with the net takes two fat marsh birds and a clutch of eggs, and you take a grazed knuckle from the stones.

The birds are plucked and cooked on the shingle before the wind turns. There is enough for the boat and a little left over; the master eats the last piece and says nothing, which is thanks enough.

watched.text:
You sit on the bow with the rope in your hand and watch the track of birds and the empty track beside it. Nobody comes down to the water. The boat waits, the wind turns, and the hour is neither lost nor spent.

When the sail goes up, the cove is already behind you.

provenance.notes: Watering and shore hunting on a coastal voyage are plausible; no specific method is claimed.
